utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar would you please call the cases.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, Mr. Dangerfield, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. And I would also urge you to try to answer the questions as precisely and as focussed as possible. And Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may continue. You received the message that you're expected to finish your cross-examination by the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I received the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dangerfield.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, I just want to cover a few things just briefly on this attack, the artillery attack on the 4th of August. Now, in an interview to the Daily Mail on the 6th of August 1995, you told the Daily Mail that you had heard that that 1800 shells went into Knin by 6.30 a.m. on the 4th of August. Did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was an exaggeration was it?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Leslie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your experience was that you had 300 shells going in, in the first half-hour. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my recollection, I believe that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just have a look. Yes. It is also in one of my reports -- my statements. Sorry, the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in your report, which is?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brief overview for Sector South on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just direct the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, general situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, so that's 300 shell in the first half-hour. So it's your testimony that 1500 shells fell between 5.30 and 6.30. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think shells and rockets would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you count them?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the information that you gave to the Daily Mail you got from Leslie that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if Leslie was wrong, of course, the information you passed on was wrong.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Leslie was wrong, yes; but I don't believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's stay with this article. Leslie also told you that the hospital had been hit, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were driving around Knin, after the -- well, when you first got out on the 7th, after the 7th of August, you saw that the hospital had not been hit. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw one side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Didn't you --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I couldn't see whether the other three sides had been hit or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you're telling us that you didn't drive around to verify whether or not the hospital had been hit. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, because the special -- the UN special envoy was there. I didn't think it was my position to be driving around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when did you go out with your guide in your Land Rover and when did you travel all around Sector South? When did that start?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two weeks -- well, as soon as I arrived in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about after the 5th of August, when did you and your driver and your Land Rover tool around, as you told us yesterday, when you saw everything that was going on in Knin and Sector South? When was that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Knin specifically on the 7th, and then Sector South from the 9th onward, once freedom of movement was re-established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So you're telling us, while you were driving around all that time, you never drove around the hospital to verify whether or not it had been hit?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go back to the hospital, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Leslie -- just staying with that for your second, Leslie also told you - this is your first statement in 1995 in paragraph 17 - that: "Colonel Leslie told me that -- about 400 body-bags in the mortuary." Do you see that, the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he say he had actually seen that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it to clarify that 400 body-bags means bags with bodies in as opposed to a pile of bags in the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So Leslie said he had seen 400 -- the information he conveyed to you was that he seen 400 body-bags with bodies in them?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my interpretation of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Did he ever tell you that: "In my previous statements ..." -- and I'm referring to Leslie's statement to the Office of the Prosecutor dated March 28th 2008. Did he ever tell that you that: "The number of bodies ..." -- in paragraph 7: "The number of bodies that I personally observed, and also indicated that the casualties from shelling were estimated to be in the hundreds, this latter estimation does not reflect my personal observation of bodies." Did he ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe, you're going at such a speed that, at a certain moment, I'm afraid that the interpreters have to translate from the transcript because their four or five lines behind, and that makes their task really far too difficulty. So you have to slow down and take a breath now and then, so that the interpreters can do the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies to the Court, the witness, and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you, sir, that this body count of 400 body-bags did not reflect his personal observations?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, staying with that, in your statement on -- not in your statement, in your article, you note - and this is on page 4 of your article, the fall of Krajina - at page 4: "Throughout the day, people went out to pick up bodies and take them into the mortuary in Knin." Now, who told that you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Canadian soldiers who went out in the APCs to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which Canadian soldiers told you that they were picking up bodies to take them to the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, Judge. I apologise. I'm sorry. My apologies, again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think specifically Colonel Steve Ferrari, but I remember other Canadians being there. I would not hazard a guess as to exactly which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Other than Corporal Ferrari, can you give us any other name?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you other names that were there, but I could give you names of the other Canadians I had worked with in my time there, and there is an possibility that they could have been amongst those who had gone out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So other than Corporal Ferrari, you don't have another name of a Canadian military member who told you that he had gone out to pick up bodies and take them to the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would be fairly certain that if others were there, it would have been Geoff Hill, Phil Berikoff, Dan Hatchi [phoen], Steve Ellis. Those -- that was the group of Canadians that I had worked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So -- so, if we went back and talked to those individuals, they would verify that they told you that they took bodies to the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm say is that I believe that they were the likely ones who would have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did they tell you how many bodies they had taken to the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me read you something from an exhibit that is in evidence, a video D329, and this is a statement by Colonel Leslie from July the 21st, 2003, talking about the shelling the Knin. "It killed a lot of civilians, and we'll never know the exact number, but estimates," estimates, "range from ten to 25.000 dead." During your entire time in the theatre, did you ever hear any estimates remotely coming close to ten to 25.000 dead, as Colonel Leslie told the folks in Canada?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me -- do you believe that number is an exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would accept that the higher end of 25.000 may be an exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell me about Leslie. Was Leslie, when he was in UN Sector South and thereafter, was he known as a person who exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me go back, if we may, briefly, and we're going back to talking about the shelling of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're going 1D42001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I direct you back to your statement of -- that's P695, your 1995 statement, at paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, no, that's -- you gave a seven-digit number, where I would expect always to be the numbers eight digits. But I now do understand it is P695. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What is on the screen is 1D42-0001, and I was directing the witness back to his statement, which is P695, paragraph 26 for reference purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just going through this, you gave six military targets in Knin, and if we can just take these on subsequently on the list, you noted, in your paragraph (c), it was the general supply depot and you gave a six-digit grid reference. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you surprised to learn that that six-digit grid reference, which is 100 metres by 100 metres, was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not surprised by a disagreement, and may I explain why?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask you which grid reference system you've overlayed on there Google picture, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me ask you this: Does it make a difference?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And explain?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. On your most basic GPS, most basic that a civilian has an access to, there are 17 different grid reference systems. These grid references can run to hundreds. I don't know whether the grid reference system you are using is British, American, Dutch, Swedish, Maidenhead, or anything else. So it is key for me to know what grid reference system you're using. May I quote -- I made some notes last night whilst I was in my hotel. May I take a piece out of my pocket and quote, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if these are the words you wrote down yesterday by yourself, then you can consult them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm preferred to give the reference where they can be found as well. The first is from -- the world headquarters for the GPS system, global positioning system, which is in Colorado in the United States, and this is from www.colorado.edu. I quote: "Referencing geodetic coordinates to the wrong data can result in position errors of hundreds of metres. Different nations and agencies use different datums as the basis for coordinate systems used to identify positions in geographic information systems, positioning systems, and navigation systems." I will also give you one shorter from Britain, the ordnance survey web site: "Standard conventions ensure only that different systems tend to agree within half a kilometre, that is 500 metres or so." So it is important that we use the right grid system on the right paper. And further to that, this is a photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you what grid system you used when you gave the grid references.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We used the WGS 84 which is the World Geodetic System 84; and Google Earth uses MGRS, which is the military grid reference system for America.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way, Mr. Kehoe, that we verify whether there are such differences? I make take it that it should not be too difficult to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It would be very easy that the grid reference system used hear is the grid reference system that was used on the mapping in UN Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether this the system you used was the grid references in the maps you used in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure because I was using British maps, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were using British maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The British maps were the maps that were used in UN Sector South. All UN Sector South mapping was produced by MOD in Britain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it appears that you're giving evidence at this moment, Mr. Kehoe. If the parties could agree on that or if the parties could look at those maps in order to ensure that not by any technical differences in similars we are misled. I'm not saying intentionally misled, but confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Kehoe. May I take it that it will be possible to make just a comparison. The witness has said what grid references he used. I think that can be verified. We can look at whether on the map we are seeing now in front of us the same are used. If not, Mr. Kehoe, I take it you could produce another map and then we will find out whether the witness was accurate or not when he gave the grid references at the time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Looking through these one by one with the grid reference, and if this is the grid reference used from the mapping system used in UN Sector South, the British mapping system, the grid reference is clearly the one you gave in "C" does not reflect that of the Senjak barracks. Now, in the Senjak barracks, you said that this -- it usually had few lightly armed soldiers wandering about. Do you see that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know that this was a -- sorry. Did you know that this was a rear command post from which troops were being deployed on the afternoon of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the next item is a grid reference that you gave which was 960755. And if that grid reference is the same -- comes from the same mapping system you used in the UN, you put that grid in the middle of the UN camp. Did you intend to talk about the camp next to the UN?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the grid I've given there would have been taken off the map that I used at the time. So, no, I didn't mean to talk about the UN, because I would have been talking about the barracks next door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next map, which is the northern barracks. That would be grid 961177. It wasn't off by much. And let us continue on with grid reference 9534758, which is your "D," and you call it an ammo dump. Now, you call this an ammo dump, and why did you call it an ammo dump, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you just tie it into the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's in paragraph 26, D. You say --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, as I continue to say there, I never saw ammunition or equipment enter or leave the storage area. And I couldn't independently verify that site because the restriction on the freedom of movement meant that I couldn't physically drive up there and identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you call it an ammo dump. Now, did you mean that was an ARSK ammunition dump?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would believe that's what I meant when I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why did you describe it as an ammunition dump?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's probably what we in the headquarters believed it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you came to that conclusion, did you have any idea what the ARSK was storing in there?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have, because I hadn't physically identified it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what was it about that location that indicated to you that it was an ammunition dump if you never saw ammunition or equipment enter or leave the storage area?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the information I gained from the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let us turn to the next item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, just for my information, you're putting to the witness, more or less, that his grid references are inaccurate in relation to the description. Now, you put on the map where the ARSK air defence battery is. Is it in evidence that it was exactly there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. It's in -- those are taken from D131 in evidence, those locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D131. I have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, pardon me. D131 does indicate that there is an air defence battery there. I don't know that it's in evidence that it actually was there; however, I do think that General Leslie did generally agree with the locations of the these air defence batteries in and around Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With this type of precision? That means that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't know that General Leslie was put to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... check on D131. please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just briefly go into private session for another frame of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is, again, the air defence battery, which is at grid reference 953758. If we could move to the next one, the next slide, which is referred to in 26A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's again a reference point with this grid reference that you have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the last slide -- excuse me, last two slides. If we can go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is it just the location of the police station which -- for which you gave no grid references.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we go to the last slide. Your Honour, I think this will be more instructive, this last slide, vis-a-vis a comparison with 131. Those are the numbers I believe that we had in 131 limited to that, and the yellow shade is the grid references given by the witness in his report. Your Honour, at this time, I will offer into evidence 1D42-0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D716, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D716 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, I think you indicated to us yesterday that you didn't know where the headquarters were for the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Were you familiar with buildings in -- in Knin that were used -- otherwise civilian buildings that you were used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm not just getting the verbatim -- that's better. Thank you. No, I was not familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you -- did you know about -- or you did know about troops moving through Knin on the 4th, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And those are moveable targets, are they not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are targets that are moving, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, of course, during the course of a military operation, those movable targets, those troops going through Knin, are legitimate targets for -- in a military operation, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Providing the risk of collateral damage is to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are they military -- is it a legitimate purpose in a military operation to attack the troops on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, I would like to point out the fact that he is certainly asking the witness for a legal conclusion, which I believe was the subject of a filing by the Defence that they did not want fact witnesses making such conclusions. Of course, if he wants that conclusion from the witness, that's fine; but I think the witness gave his answer, that it's not a yes-or-no question and that there are other considerations to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. At the same time, is it a legitimate purpose in a military operation to attack the troops on the other side? Mr. Kehoe, that's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As a soldier, is it a legitimate purpose in a military operation to attack soldiers on the other side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, it is it, of course, a legal question, but it is a totally unnecessary question. It is the same as: Is the purpose of being a milkman to deliver milk? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I take that as a yes, Your Honour, and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you say in your statement, at paragraph 32, that you never saw any other RSK military targets being hit. When you say that, it's because that you didn't actually observe individual military targets being hit, not that they weren't hit. Isn't that right. Let me help you out, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw military targets. Sorry. Do you just want to rewind and rephrase the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, you say, in paragraph 32, that -- in the middle of paragraph 32: "Apart from the police station, I never saw any other ARSK military targets being hit." You're not saying that they weren't hit; you just didn't see them. Right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that may be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you took a ride around Knin on the 7th and thereafter. And I -- I take it you were in communications with various individuals who were likewise riding around Knin and examining damage from the shelling. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you didn't talk to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, if the senior -- by the way, did you yourself do any crater analysis on any of the shelling that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not whilst I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you do it afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you never did?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So did you ever have a conversation with -- and let me go through this. This is it from P64, where the Senior Military Observer concluded that, in general, the shelling was concentrated against military targets. That was in his provisional report, and that was in P64. And that there was, likewise, a final assessment, and this comes from the statement of Mr. Roberts on the 23rd of July, 2008. This is page - I'm looking for the page - 7022, from line 19, where he says: "I am aware that a final assessment was sent. "Question: Are you aware that the final assessment was sent by UNMO. "Answer: I think, at the time, a final assessment report was being sent to Zagreb headquarters. I think we had several conversations in the UNMO office about the further assessment to be the one I was shown now in terms of August 18th." And in those -- this is moving on to 7022, line 1: "And in those conversations with UNMOs, at the time, they told you that the further assessment was consistent with the initial assessment. Isn't that correct?" "I think I recall seeing the final document ..." -- this was the answer: "I think I recall seeing the final document that went up and that it concurred with their final assessment." Were you aware of that assessment being done by the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that it was their job to do such an assessment, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the individual UNMOs -- or, rather, the UNMOs mandate was because I was not an UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, were you aware that the UN CIVPOL did a similar assessment with a similar result?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one second here, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will come back to this issue in a moment when we find a another exhibit, but let me just move ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps, meanwhile, you referred me to D131, where, in a map prepared by the Defence, C3 is indicated on that map. You said, well, that's the evidence of Mr. Leslie. I read on page 2134, line 8 and 9, as one of the answers of the then-witness: "Yes, sir. The only reason why I asked for a little bit," let me just read it, "more specificity. I can't recall if that is the exact location of C3. I was pointing at differences, apparent inaccuracies." Now you further referred me to another witness, and we don't have to go into precise session, but it must be the evidence given on the 23rd, 26th, or 27th of May, and I'd like to have the page and line reference for where that witness gave the exact location for C3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going have to get that. But I will say to Your Honour, at this point, that the reference in these grid references that we've been looking at here in -- I will provide that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about grid references. I'm talking about what we exactly have in evidence as to the exact location of the installations this witness referred to. He gave grid reference whether they are accurate or not. Of course, on a map, if you compare that, it should be beyond any doubt that the location indicated on the map where they really were found is correct. I asked: Is this in evidence? You referred me to the testimony of Mr. Leslie. And upon checking this, I primarily find that on the basis of a map the Defence has produced, Mr. Leslie says, "I'm not sure whether this is the exact location yes or no." So, therefore, the second source you gave me, which is three full days of transcript, I'd like to receive a bit more guidance on where we find that. And I take it that are you not a position to immediately do that, and we'd like to receive that, for example, after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir, after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, by the way, sir, when you were in Sector South --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me pull up a photograph, and that would be D83.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, that's you to the right in that photograph, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So, if someone identified you to that regard, they would be mistaken?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say almost certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let us -- when you were driving around, sir, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could the witness perhaps tell us, if it is not him, whether he knows who it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. In fact, I have never seen them before in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were driving around, sir, in looking at the damage in Knin -- well, let me backtrack. You said, during the course of your testimony on direct, that there was no fighting withdrawal. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you were driving around, you noted for us that you saw damage, shelling damage. How much of that shelling damage was caused by the ARSK firing toward Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the ARSK didn't fire towards Knin, nor did they fire out of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us take a look at D89, a sitrep of 5 August 1995. And if we could -- after the cover page, if we could go four pages in. Can we blow up that -- at 5th of August at 1500. It's the third paragraph down. Scroll that up gist a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "1500 ARSK soldiers of unknown strength seen occupying defence positions in the general area of Strmica. Tanks and mortars were in the same positions. On the 5th at 1815, they fired 12 rounds of artillery from Strmica towards Knin." Now, by that time, sir, by 1815, the HV was in Knin, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just going to read the paragraph again. By 1815, on the 5th, yes, I would agree, the HV were in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, based on this UNMO -- excuse me, on this Sector South report, reporting this shelling, you just didn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who made this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can I go to the front page, sir, of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we go to the front page, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean which nation reported it, not who drafted the assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just page through this, page 1, page 2, and this is begins --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It starts with the Kenyan battalion. Going on to the next page, it is a continuation of the Kenyan battalion before it gets to the Canadian battalion.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it has come from the Kenyan, the information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that, because I didn't see it. I didn't see the artillery firing from the Strmica area, so I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if -- you also -- if there is shelling coming into Knin from the RSK on the 5th, you don't know as you drive through Knin which damage is caused by HV shelling and which damage is caused by ARSK shelling, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you could have a good guess if you did the crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you didn't do that --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you -- I'm sorry. You didn't do that, so you don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell the difference. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one final issue before we end, and I want to ask you a general question. It emanates -- and I would like to read this to you. It emanates from a London Times article of 19 December 1988. -- excuse me, 1998. I apologise. Thank you. And it talks about an investigation done by the Times, and reads as follows: "A Times investigation has revealed that a man's real name," this man Lawson, "appears nowhere in UN records -- UN records headquarters. He was never an official employee, was not recruited locally, and was not an officer in any UN peacekeeping force." By the way, this article discusses generally that MI6 agents representing themselves as UN peacekeepers planted articles in the British press in an effort to counter widespread sympathy for Bosnian Muslims ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it up there? That's fine. We can put it over on Sanction, so that the witness can read it. We can just have the witness read this on Sanction. We are not going to cover it, Judge, but it just may be easier for the witness to read. If we can scroll down that little bit. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I just read for you is that matter beginning: "The Times investigation ..." Continuing with the next paragraph : "Balkans experts have observed that the articles sought to counter widespread sympathy for the Bosnian Muslims by pointing out that atrocities occurred on all sides, a point of view consistent with that expressed by many in the British military and the Foreign Office." Tell me, Mr. Dangerfield, during the course of your time in either Gornji Vakuf, Split, or Knin, were you ever instructed by any superior to play up, if you will, evidence of crimes committed by Croats or Bosnian Muslims in an effort to counter widespread sympathy for either?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you Mr. Dangerfield.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I clarify one point on the grid reference system? I think it is important to note, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think it would assist the Chamber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, sir. Irrespective of whether the grid reference systems are the same, the application of that grid reference system is used for a topographical map, i.e., one that you and I would use to map read along a road. It doesn't matter what scale it is. That grid reference system has been applied to a photograph that doesn't take topographical inaccuracies into account. So the grid reference system, whether it is the same or not, is being used incorrectly in this case, and that would account for any inaccuracies in my grids, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you have a kind of a general explanation for all inaccuracies. Are there inaccuracies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are inaccuracies. And you say it's the way in which, where you earlier said that the grid systems were not the same, that you say apparently now that they may be the same but are applied in a different way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are all sort of inaccuracies that can be accounted for, sir, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So how are they applied in a different way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's all based around what type of map used. If you look in an atlas, sir, there are a lot of different pictures of the world and the countries, particularly at the beginning. And they're different projections of maps, and they're called Mercator, Stereographic, Cylindrical, Conical. The correct grid system has to be applied to the correct map; otherwise, Rome could indeed be in New York, and New York could indeed be in Rome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, of course, I said that yesterday in relation to scales. By the way, I think I made a mistake because Rome would then be in the same grid reference as New York. If we're talking about scales, Rome would still be different from New York. But the more precise the maps are, isn't it, the less the influence of technical aspects of how the grid references are applied. And we are talking here about quite detailed maps. So, if you say I have got a general explanation for all of the inaccuracies, then one of the things that strikes me first is that the inaccuracies seem to be of a different dimension, one time far away on the same map, relatively nearby. So I would expect inaccuracies then to have a systematic effect on what we see, and not one time two, three, or four wrong grid references in the system we're using with six -- six digits and another time relatively nearby. Do you have an explanation for the differences in the inaccuracies you say are explained by a general explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you make a very fair point, sir. I think another point to note is that when using my map, I would have been working off kilometre grid squares and perhaps might not have used the compass to tie it down to exact hundred metre positioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you have given three explanations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You started saying that we had different grid systems. The second explanation was that the grid systems may be the same, when I asked the Defence to verify, but that they are applied in a different way. And now I asked you, whether this general explanation, how that could apply where the inaccuracies are of a different dimension. And now you say you might have made mistakes yourself. So we have at least now three different explanations for the inaccuracies. The further explanation, does that need any further questions to the witness, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we're moving the furniture to whom Mr. Cayley brought his own furniture. Mr. Cayley, will you be the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will you now be cross-examined by Mr. Cayley, who is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, I have now much to ask you, probably about half an hours worth. I'm right in saying that you were tasked by Brigadier-General Alain Forand to gather intelligence or information in Sector South, is that right, in pursuance of the mission of UNCRO in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He described me as his one-man reconnaissance regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that headquarters, the UNCRO Sector South headquarters, would also provide you with information of what was taking place in Sector South. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a two-way process.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that kind of information that they provided to you and you provided to them would have been information concerning movement of military personnel. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And subject matter such as freedom of movement within Sector South. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, what I wanted to you do now is actually direct your mind specifically to the issue of freedom of movement; and if could you, please, turn to page 3 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is P695. It is actually number 2 at the bottom, but it is page 3 of the purposes of the document actually uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is paragraph 9. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you note, in your statement, that: "Restriction of movement between the 7th and 8th of August of 1995 remains fierce with many UN personnel confined to camp."

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, by all means, read the rest of that paragraph, if you want to. I don't want to ask you more questions about it, but I do actually want to now show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, P29 could be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the human rights action team, HRAT, do you remember their activities in Sector South during your time there; Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never heard the name Flynn before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now you can see a report there from the Human Rights Action Team. This is a daily report dated 8th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now I'm not so much interested that you didn't know the existence of HRAT, but the paragraph in this report that I would like you to look at is the paragraph that beginnings: "Freedom of movement."

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you read that, and I'm actually interested in the last sentence after that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Movement today has been restricted ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You don't read to read it. Just read it to yourself. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now the last sentence will you see is stating that General Cermak delivered a written statement to General Forand this morning that movement tomorrow to Drnis would be possible and HRAT intends to test this assurance. Do you recall if around that time, the 8th of August, UNCRO and another international organisations were authorised to travel between Knin and Drnis?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that exactly. I do remember at some stage a written document. I believe, from memory, it was signed by General Cermak, and I -- referring to freedom of movement. The actual detail of that, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at P513. Can you look at that document? Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could we have the English version, please, next to the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. This specific one, I don't recall. I think it's too specific. I remember one, I think, of a more general nature throughout the sector. So I don't recall this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just for clarity sake, do you recall around the 8th of August that the restrictions on movement were lifted on the road between Knin and Drnis?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, the witness could be shown map 21. This is the bundle, Your Honours, which is the Prosecution bundle of maps. I don't think it has been uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify this issue, matters of freedom of movement like this - I know you can't recall now - this was the kind of information that you would have received from Sector South headquarters and General Forand, if, indeed, he had been informed?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying that on the 9th of August, you travelled to Kistanje. Yeah?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you orient yourself on this map. Do you see Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And do you see Drnis? It is south. It's a blue dot to the south, and we'll put it on the ELMO so the Judges can see once you've --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the blue dot to the right of Rivnik [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you looking at map 21?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To the south of Knin, you'll see Drnis. It is just above the scale at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There's no grid references, thank goodness, on this map, so we don't need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If could you put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And can you just indicate to the Judges the road between Knin and Drnis.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the previous document that we just looked at, but which you were not aware of, appeared to give or at least lift restriction of movement on the road between Knin and Drnis. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you point out to the judges the town of Kistanje which you visited on the 9th of August. It is, in fact, west.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Keep going. Down. There.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you ask the witness to show Kistanje to the Judges. The Judges have seen this map many, many times. Then you guide the witness to where Kistanje is, which is, of course, a bit of an old exercise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't think there is a dispute as to where Kistanje is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now you would accept that Kistanje is not actually on the road between Knin and Drnis, is it?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, in fact, even though freedom of movement had not been granted in that area, it appears that you were unaffected by the restriction of movement that still existed in the Kistanje area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could please turn back to your statement, P695, page 4, paragraph 12. And these are just some clarifications where I want you to refer to your supplementary statement that you made to Mr. Russo. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You made some additions. I just wanted to get that on the record. That's all.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You'll see it says there on the 10th of August: "UN personnel met with General Cermak requesting complete freedom of movement throughout Sector South. He says he cannot authorise this. It must come from his higher commander." Now, in your supplementary statement, you identify who you believe actually passed that information to you. Do you have a copy of your supplementary information sheet? I can give that to you.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's on the second page of the supplementary information sheet.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know the supplementary sheet, that is the one submitted two days ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, it is actually not in evidence. It is simply information passed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that in my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't include that in the documents I gave to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can read it to you so we don't waste any time. You say in that that supplementary information sheet that that piece of information on General Cermak being unable to authorise freedom of movement came from either Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk, Colonel Leslie, or General Forand. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would point more towards Colonel Tymchuk --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who gave that you pieces of information?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the letter granting freedom of movement throughout the Sector South area that was signed by General Cermak, you said, in your supplementary information sheet, it was not worth the paper that it was printed on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like me to clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you some questions. Is that because you were unable to pass through check-points with a copy of that letter?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And by which type of personnel were those check-points manned by? Were they military personnel?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a combination of military and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything else --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military police, as well. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the check-points that you couldn't get through with that letter were manned by HV military, HV military police, and civilian police. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you would like to add to that, or is that clear?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, some check-point would say let you through, some check-points wouldn't. And, therefore, that, to me, indicated that actually, I think, the message hadn't got out to everywhere, and that's quite understandable when not everyone has a radio. When not everyone has a telephone, it is difficult getting that information out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Dangerfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Before we continue, I have one question for you, Mr. Kehoe. Let me just find the ... On page 19, line 15, we're talking about photograph D83, you said: "So if someone identified you to that regard, that would be mistaken." That puzzled me, because it raised on my mind a question whether anyone had identified Mr. Dangerfield as the person on the right of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who did that and when?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My recollection, and I would have to look back specifically, but it was in talking to Mr. Munkelien and Mr. Anttila. We asked who it was, and they said it was the British officer that was in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we have is we have the testimony of Mr. Munkelien, who said: "It was the British officer, but I don't know his name." So "the British officer" is not for me the exactly the same as "Mr. Dangerfield." Now Mr. Hill testified that it was a Czech captain. So, therefore, it puzzled me what made you so positive to already mention an identification. Mr. Hill said it was a Czech captain or it was a major pilot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, the issue is we have not been able to identify this person, and this is the British officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. My issue at this moment is that you suggest that there was an identification on rather loose grounds. Please proceed, but, of course, not you, at this moment. Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Dangerfield, is counsel for Mr. Markac, and he will now cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dangerfield.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm looking for my pen. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, again. I would like to ask you a few questions on the topic that was indicated at the beginning and that remained, at least in my view, not completely clarified. Originally, you came to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the end of April 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your statement, P695 - that's the first statement from 1995 - you stated that you had worked in section G2 with the British forces in Gornji Vakuf. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't work in the G2 section, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] I will show you your statement on page 1, paragraph 1, where it says: "I was the British Army SLO based in Knin working in the British G2 cell."

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I've got it. Yeah. I mean, I was sector liaison officer. That was my prime role. And as a by-product, the information I was providing would have gone to the G2 cell to help build up the picture. So, whilst not directly employed by the G2, I provided information to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. You now referring to the time between the 4th and the 10th of August, 1995, when you were in Knin. However, I'm asking after your arrival to the territory of the former Yugoslavia, in end April 1995, to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina that is, within which force did you act, which organisation, what was its complement, and what was your position within it? Could you please describe.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was within the sector liaison organisation. From recollection, there was probably a dozen of us from across -- mainly the army and mainly the Royal Marines. In fact, I think all the drivers were from the Royal Marines. And we were deployed initially as liaison officers. I think we were more working directly for the brigadier, Brigadier Pringle, in Gornji Vakuf, and we went to the various battalions in Sector South West. So, initially, I worked in Tomislavgrad and I worked in Vitez and the surrounding areas as a liaison officer, and my job was to try to set up meetings between the senior military commanders and Brigadier Pringle. So we had the credibility of having the brigadiers' ear, and the important think was to try to cut through the bureaucracy, which we all experience, to go straight to the senior military commanders and set up those meetings. So that was, initially, what I did until I was moved to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Were you then working within the UNPROFOR in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the mandate of the UNPROFOR at the time was relatively vague in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and was, in fact, to try to moderate between the warring sides to achieve a cease-fire and a cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact mandate. What I do remember was I was a 25-year-old captain doing what his superior officers had asked him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that your superior officer was Brigadier Pringle. Was he the one who sent you to Knin, to the commander of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did that mean that, after your arrival at Knin, you transferred to the subordination of General Forand or did you remain subordinated to Brigadier Pringle?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was a specific transfer of my subordination. I don't think you would -- I don't -- I am fairly certain there was no documentation to support that, but I think it was -- I think in British terms you would call it a gentleman's agreement between the two Brigadiers, that I would work for General Forand, yet effectively still be under the command of Brigadier Pringle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would I be mistaken if I said that your position within Sector South at the UNCRO base in Knin was, in a certain way, exceptionally? And I am referring to the fact that you had your own vehicle and a driver at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You wouldn't be mistaken. I thought I was unbelievably lucky to have such responsibility at that age.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have told us that the vehicle you used to tour the terrain was a Land Rover. Could you tell us how it was marked. What colour was it and what were the licence plates?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The licence -- wrong. The colour of the Land Rover was white, UN white. I can't -- I'm fairly certain we probably had some shabby looking UN stickers, blue ones on it. And I simply can't remember what the registration of the vehicle was. I can't remember whether it was British or, indeed, it had UN on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Apart from you, and, of course, General Forand, commander of the Sector South, was there any other person in the command who had a vehicle and a driver at their service?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fairly certain people like Colonel Leslie and Colonel Tymchuk had those sort of assets. I mean, there's nothing unusual about me having a vehicle and a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'll refer back to your statement, P695, where, at the beginning, you said that before coming to the territory of the former Yugoslavia, you had undergone certain preparations; namely, you completed a one-week UNMO course and a one-week sector liaison officer course. That's a total of two weeks of familiarizing yourself with the terrain you were going to cover. Was that all the education you received for that assignment or was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was it. And I was fairly unique in having done both those courses, and that's because they couldn't make up their minds as to how they were going to deploy me. Initially, they thought I would deploy as an UNMO, because earlier on in the year, I think there were many potential agreements between the warring factions. And the British were lining up to deploy ten or 15 UNMOs at short notice, and so I went on that course. Then the potential agreement fell apart, so I think I did nothing for three months, until the brigade that I was with in Germany deployed, and the Brigadier said, "I'll take Dangerfield as a sector liaison officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That course, among other things, included, as we can see in point "A," FRY vehicle/aircraft/weapon systems recognition. At the time, it was the Federal Republic Of Yugoslavia, indeed. Did that course include recognition of the same, in the system of the Republic of Croatia, military vehicles, police vehicles, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: From recollection, yes. I mean, I think the aim was it was to give an overview and identify the detail across all of former warring factions, and I think licence plates -- from memory, I think the Croatia plates were yellow with -- the Croatian military with yellow with black numbers and letters. I think they all had different ones, and I think it pretty critical to be able to tell the deference between the two -- oh, sorry, difference between the three different sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Within that course, were you made aware of the structure of the Croatian army, the civilian police, military police, the special police, the system of civil protection? Did you familiarize yourself with the structure and the composition of the organisations that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fairly certain I did. I wouldn't be able to do for you now. I think that is a standard procedure for the British Army whenever it deploys, as it would do for Iraq, as it would do for Afghanistan. It is part of our general education and preparation to make sure that we are equipped mentally and physically to deal with whatever is thrown at you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you able at the time to distinguish among members of different agencies according to uniform or vehicle they were driving?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I clarify agencies as battalions and brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When I mentioned agencies I meant, on the one hand, Croatian army, on the other hand, military police, as opposed to special police and regular police. Were you able to distinguish between members of these various agencies, according to their appearance?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is it a good moment to make a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will have a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dangerfield, I will now refer to paragraph 2 of your statement from 1995 - that's P695 - where you described your duties from the 4th to the 10th of August, 1995. You say that you were supposed to report on every incident, an action by both HV and ARSK troops; that you were working with both UK and SS G2 cells; that you were trying to build up a certain picture of HV intentions, ARSK reactions and future operations by both sides. And this would help the British G2 in Gornji Vakuf to work out what effect this would have on western Bosnia. Do you agree with this description of your assignments in your statement? Would you still say the same today?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, I would agree with it. I would say, perhaps, that the last sentence, "This would help the British G2 in Sector South West work out what effect this would have on western Bosnia," is a little bit grand perhaps, and perhaps not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that? Why do you think so today?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose one would like to think I have matured over 13 years, and when I read that again, I was looking at gathering information, to be honest wherever I was and wherever I went. And to suspect that the G2 cell could work out what strategic effect this would have on western Bosnia is perhaps a little bit grand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As you arrived in Knin - that is, before Operation Storm - I suppose you were made aware of the UNCRO mandate, and that was to demilitarise the area of the so-called Serbian Republic of Krajina, putting it under control, and monitoring military movements along the border of that area. Were you made aware that mandate of the UNCRO in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was probably made aware of it by the Sector South headquarters. I think, specifically, I would have been interested in the aspect of monitoring military movements along the border area, I think known as the Zone of Separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the registrar to pull up D28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will now see, Mr. Dangerfield, one document that has been exhibited already, and that's the agreement between the government of the Republic of Croatia and the peace forces of the United Nations. The UNCRO concluded on the 6th of August, 1995; that is to say, after Operation Storm had been launched on the 4th of August. Were you familiar with this document? Have you had the opportunity to see it or read it before?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with it, and I don't believe I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like us to focus on paragraph 2 of this document - that's page 2 in Croatian - describing the mandate. Please look at it, Mr. Dangerfield. In this paragraph, the definition of the UNCRO mandate at the level between the Republic of Croatia and the peace forces of the UN was signed by Mr. Saranic on behalf of the Croatian government and by Mr. Yasushi Akashi on behalf of the UN. You mentioned that the latter had visited Knin. This agreement actually changes the mandate of the UNCRO, and reorients it towards humanitarian affairs and human rights -- the human rights situation. Were you informed by anyone in Sector South of this change of mandate of the UNCRO, beginning with the 6th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I probably had been made aware of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, despite that, you continue to perform duties such as monitoring military movements of the HV and the RSK army, trying to deduce their intentions in various military interventions and how that would reflect on the situation in western Bosnia. That does not seem to be in conformity with this changed mandate of the UNCRO as specified in this agreement. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part. I conformed with my superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Para 11 of your statement of 1995, you say that from the European Monitors you received certain information about various personalities in the Croatian army, and you mention General Gotovina, General Cermak. And in paragraph -- in item C, that is, you refer to officer Ivan Juric, Major Ivan Juric. You say that he drove a black Mercedes with a certain registration plate, that he was working at the barracks in Zagreb, and you mention his phone number. Mr. Dangerfield, have you ever met personally with Major Ivan Juric?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what you intended when you said he was chief of police? What does that mean? Which police do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That's the information I got from the European Community monitors. So I don't know which police, special police, military police, civilian police. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 22, in your statement, says that on the 27th of July, Radio Knin announced a full mobilisation of the army of the RSK, and you go on to say what it included in points A through D. Did you hear this announcement yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would have been in the B/C/S, and, therefore, it would have been a translation that was handed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who gave you information about this announcement?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 23, you say, at that time, Knin was almost empty as far as men of military age are concerned, and that you had very good freedom of movement in view of the panic that occurred, and you say that on the 27th, all the fire engines seemed to be filling up at the petrol observation. Was that your personal observation or was it taken from a sitrep or another report?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe if it is written like that. I would have seen that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your explanation for this behaviour by the firemen on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be my assessment, and opinion only, that the fire brigade were preparing for some kind of attack. It is unusual for fire engines all to be filling up at the same time, and so I assess that they were expecting something. And there was a shortage of fuel, I believe, in Knin, so I would assume they were filling up whilst they still had fuel available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. There's just one thing that I won't say bothers me, but makes me curious. In paragraph 29, you say that there was a restriction of movement and UN personnel was confined to camp. What do you mean by "confined "?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us were allowed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were not "allowed out," who was it that did not allow you to leave the UN base?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As this was on the 4th of August, it would have been the ARSK soldiers who were at the front gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, in paragraph 9, reference is made to the period of the 7th and 8th of August; in other words, at the time when the Croatian army troops enter the Knin. Would you like me to reiterate my question, Mr. Dangerfield?
