We've placed this statement of yours in a time-frame, and my question was: When you said that you were not allowed to leave the camp, who was it that did not allow to you leave the UN base?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th, and I suppose up to the early hours or the early morning of the 5th of August, it would have been the ARSK soldiers, and then it was either the soldiers who were killed or the soldiers which you will have read in my statement, or it would have been soldiers who had left shortly prior to the Croatian soldiers' arrival. So, whilst there was probably no overlap between the two by minutes, I suspect the time-frame between the two was not that long. So, for the 1st, I suppose, up until the middle of the 5th, it would have been ARSK soldiers preventing us from getting out; and when the Croatian soldiers arrived on the 5th, it was they who prevented us from getting out. Indeed, they tried to get into the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see document 3D00-1760.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will see, in a moment, Mr. Dangerfield, an article published on the 6th of August, 1995 in the Sunday Mail or Mail on Sunday. And in this article, reference is made to your statements. And if we now turn to page 2 of this document, the paragraph before last, we can see that it states the following. Your statement is quoted here, and it reads as follows: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "... agreed no one would leave the compound, and the Croats promised not to enter the camp." [Interpretation] Am I wrong if I conclude based on this that the issue of UN personnel and their confinement to the UN base in Knin was agreed in a mutual agreement between the Croatian army and the command of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this incident very well because the Croatian soldiers tried to force their way into the camp. And it was the first time in my military career that I had been told to cock my weapon and be required to use it if necessary, and the reason for why is that the British Army rules of engagement were more robust than the Canadian army rules of engagement. So, if necessary, I would have used the force required of me by the superior officer to prevent that happening. Once it was understood by the Croatian soldiers the enormity of the situation, my superior officers and whoever the senior Croatian soldier or officer who was at the front gate, I believe this agreement came into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. How, then, am I to interpret in this context the quotes in the paragraph before this one where you state, speaking of Croatian soldiers: "They were friendly [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... and that sort of thing."

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the appearance of the soldiers overall was that they were happy with their achievements, and, therefore, their demeanour was friendly, they were firing their rifles into the air, and that's how they behave. But it's different --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I would now like to refer you to your second statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness had not finished his answer where you said: "But it's different ..." Could you please complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But it is different to when you have a UN compound with a whole load of civilians in who are not under the UN badge, and that, I believe, was the issue which caused the standoff at the front gate to the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be that as it may, however, is it correct that when you said that agreement was reached between the Croatian army and the UN, according to which the Croatian army would not enter the base and the UN personnel would not leave the base, so was this agreement reached or not? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, would you please take a look at paragraph 8 of your 2008 statement, the statement of January of this year. In paragraph 8, you say that you personally observed HV soldiers standing around in towns and villages where houses and crops or stables were burning, and also that you saw members of the Croatian special police preventing access to areas that were burning. I would now like to us to talk about this part of your statement. First of all, could you tell us when was it that you observed this situation? What time-period was this in?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would have been the two weeks after August the 9th, from August the 9th onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what area you're referring to when you say "around in towns and villages." Which areas do you have in mind? Which town precisely or which village?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them in the area that was known as Sector South. I mean, it was throughout Sector South; and as I said in the previous paragraph, 80 to 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I wasn't quite clear, so I will reiterate my question. Are you referring here to -- are you saying that the special police prevented entry into or access to villages and towns in the entire area?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they probably dealt with one -- well, I mean, I don't know how many special police there were, but I think they probably dealt with each village or town when they could; and, therefore, I couldn't be in the whole area at the same time. But they certainly seemed to be present in quite a few areas that I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you're unable to tell us how many members of the special police there were. You cannot tell us where these things happen. You say probably throughout the area. And, of course, you're also saying that you could not be present in all these places that you have -- that you visited. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct when you say how many -- I can't tell you how many members of the special police there were. And, in fact, I haven't given specific grid references in this statement to everywhere that I saw on fire because they were too numerous to list. And if I could give an analogy, after the Iraq war, the oil wells were set on fire and I think we probably all saw those on television. If you were to replace those oil wills with a village, a town, a settlement, that is what the area looked like. It was all on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, in your 2008 statement, when, in paragraph 8, you speak of these events, you were, in fact, in a way, motivated by what you experienced in Iraq a few years later. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't in Iraq at that time of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When were you in Iraq, Mr. Dangerfield?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just work it out. I have to think back where I've been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the witness compared what he saw with what he now says he apparently saw on the television as oil wills burning. Now, is there any specific reason why we -- because that has got nothing to do, I understand, with his presence in Iraq. Is there any specific reason why we have to explore his presence in Iraq. If there is, please proceed; if there's not, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From my point of view, a very strange experience that someone experience, which took place after the events that he is talking about in his statement, could be relevant for the references in the statement of the events that happened long before the period that he has talk about his experience. So this is kind of odd for me, but I will pass on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the witness only today explained to us that it had a similar look as what he once saw, apparently after the events. It could be before as a matter of fact. Because while the Iraq war, I take it that Mr. Dangerfield is referring to the war where Iraq was attacking one of its neighbouring countries, and not the war in which Iraq was attacked later. But apart that from that, he is just referring to what it looked like, and I think there's -- I was already a bit surprised that you said, Did it inspire you? He just made a comparison. Nothing more, nothing less, as far as I'm concerned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will go on, Your Honour. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your supplement statement to the Prosecutor a few days ago, you also referred to this paragraph of your 2008 January statement, and you said there that members of the special police personally prevented you from getting out. Was this -- does this mean that this is your own personal experience and not something that you have learned about second-hand?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think I explained it at the end of the Prosecution's questioning, and that was specifically in the area of Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Of?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I think I refer to it in - I think - in the article I wrote, The Fall of The Republic Of Serbian Krajina. I think I probably refer to it in there, and I think I call it on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe can you help us with this, because I can't recall seeing anything, any mention of this topic in your article?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 6, paragraph 2, that begins: "Other patrols saw us ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] But I can't see here that you make mention of the special police.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As you said, then, you had personal contact with them. Could you tell us, then, whether you spoke with any of these members of the special police who prevented you from accessing this area?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- I only had a limited grasp of B/C/S, as did my driver. I had no interpreter. It's amazing what you can understand through sign language and gestures with the hands and the small amount of B/C/S that I spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is, of course, quite clear. How was this person that you say was a special police member, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said earlier on under cross-examination that whilst during the deployment or prior to the deployment, we had been briefed and taught what people wore; and, of course, I knew that throughout my tour. Thirteen years on, I can't -- I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you at least remember whether he was wearing civilian clothing or a uniform?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It almost certainly was a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, just in general terms, what the pattern on the uniform was?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I'm not going to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this person of whom you say was a special police officer armed?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you always respect someone who has -- is equipped with a weapon; and, therefore, if I was escorted out of the sector, if I was prevented from going somewhere, it normally meant they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did this person have?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I was briefed prior to deployment on all sorts of various different weapons; and, of course, there are weapons that are prolific throughout the world, and so it was likely to have been weapons of small calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you mean a short barrel or long barrel?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think everyone was equipped with pistols and rifles. When I say "everyone," I mean generically throughout the Balkans. I cannot tie to special police different units whether they had a pistol or a rifle. My memory simply isn't that good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, a lot of time has passed. Do you recall this event that you say was in Cetina, an event where you were stopped and prevented to enter this area by a unit that you say were special police? Was this a check-point where you were stopped, or were you stopped by some other means?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think somewhere I refer to not being noticed for a while, which may have meant that I hadn't got as far as a check-point, I was short of a check-point. Just because I wasn't at a check-point, it doesn't mean there was no check-point. I had got myself into a position where I could view what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, do you remember whether, during your stay and mandate in Sector South, you had contacts with any official officers of the special police?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the role of the special police was in Operation Storm and following Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, of course, it's been a long time, and it's quite understandable when you say that you cannot remember today all the things that you knew at that time; in other words, in August 1995. However, could you please explain why it is that you mentioned this event, where you were prevented by the special police to enter certain areas; whereas, in your statement of January of this year and your supplemental statement of July of this year, no mention, not a single word, is said about these events in 1995 in your statement of 1995, where, of course, your memories would have been much fresher. Could you please explain there?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason why I mentioned it initially is because it was, to me and my driver, an event that was potentially life threatening, at the time. But it was an event, and over the years one just moves on from these things. It is no longer an event, it's an event in my past. One moves on. It's history . It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Dangerfield, but you still haven't answered how come you don't mention it in 1995, when it was fresh in your mind and when you would have been able to describe that person, both in terms of appearance, uniform, the weapon he was carrying, and other details. But 13 years later you do mention it in your statement to the Prosecution; and in doing so, you referred to the member -- to a member of the special police, although you can't any longer remember what the attributes of the special police were.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're getting muddled here. I mentioned this event in Cetina. Yes, I don't mention the special police specifically. But this article which was written no less than ten days afterwards was a general account of my experiences. It was, as can you read, written by a young man who was very impressionable and keen to partake of his experiences with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Let's move on to a different subject. That's precisely the article you were talking about, P699. You authored this article which was written, as you said, some ten days after the event in Knin for a -- the British Army Review. What kind of publication is that, just to give us a picture? What is the readership of this review?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a magazine that is printed, I believe, a couple of times a year, and it's where officers and soldiers of the British Army can write about military affairs, whether past, present, or future. It's a medium for discussion. And, at the time, some people described me as the most shelled officer, i.e., the man who had been under the most incoming rocket and artillery fire since the Second World War. So it was of interest to people. And whilst I wrote this account for myself, I decided to send it in to the editor of the magazine to share that experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've just answered a question I haven't yet asked. So it was on your own initiative that you sent the article to that magazine. Nobody asked you to do so, right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, however, the witness has not answered the question that you did put to him; that is, what is the readership. Who are the readers of this magazine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the armed forces and the wider defence community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go through this article. In the introduction, you say that starting with May of that year, 1995, your job was to monitor the build-up of Croatian forces in the south and south-east of Sector South, and in the west as well of Sector South. And you had also been monitoring the response to this by the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. However, what I am interested in is your reference to the fact that negotiations had begun between Croats, led by Franjo Tudjman, and the Serbs, led by Milan Martic. Mr. Dangerfield, do you know, at least the basic features of plan Z-4?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I told you that plan Z-4 was an attempt, a joint attempt at the time by the European Community, Russia, and the US, to reintegrate peacefully the territory of the so-called RSK into the Republic of Croatia, would that jog your memory a bit?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me strategic and political question, which I can't possibly answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, Mr. Mikulicic is asking you whether you knew what plan Z-4 was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Mr. Mikulicic, then gave a little sketch of what Z-4 was in his view, and asked whether that refreshed your recollection. That's not a political question. That is not a strategic question. That is a question about whether this refreshes your memory, whether you have any knowledge yes or no. If have you, please tell us; if it doesn't refresh your memory, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I refer in the article somewhere that I talk about the peaceful reintegration of the Republica Serb Krajina. I didn't know it was specifically Z-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, even if you didn't know it was plan Z-4, you were aware that some sort of negotiations were -- peace negotiations were going on between Zagreb and Knin, and I'm referring to paragraph 2 on page 2 of your article.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Dangerfield, who Mr. Leonid Kerestedzijanc was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerestedzijanc was the first Russian Ambassador to the Republic of Croatia; and along with Mr. Peter Galbraith, he played a major role in the attempt to realise the Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have 3D00-0777 called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will now show you an article published in the Croatian press, in February last year, an interview with Mr. Kerestedzijanc where he mentions the plan Z-4 and the reaction of Milan Martic to the negotiations about this plan. I'll refer you just to one portion of that article that is relevant for our purposes, where it is said that upon his arrival to Knin, Mr. Kerestedzijanc, who had previously talked to Mr. Tudjman as well, had wanted to hand over the plan for reintegration without any conflict to Mr. Martic; whereas, the latter answered briefly, "We just won't take that into our hands," and that put[paid to any peaceful negotiations. Do you know from any other source about the response of then-authorities in Knin to the peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I think I earlier expressed that this courtroom is not a place where we inform witnesses about events, but that this is a place where witnesses still the Court what they've observed so that the Court can make the determinations. I must say the quantity of rather long questions, including documents, including plans, et cetera, which ones asked to the witness if he knows anything about and the answer is "no" and then the next series, is not something that the Chamber considers to be of great assistance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will go on, Your Honour. I will tender this as a document, please, as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, under the standard the Court applied with respect to the Fisk article, I don't know that this article really has any foundation to come in. The witness doesn't know anything about it, doesn't indicate that he is quoting anything, a party of the case. So, on that basis, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, in what respect is this different from the Fisk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say that on his article, in page 2, the witness is referring to the peace negotiations between Krajina officials and representative of the Croatian government, and he is also referring to the visit Mr. Akashi to Knin, and he is also referring to the Geneva peace talk negotiations, which are all very, very close connected to the Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Although the witness is not ware specifically of what the Z-4 plan means, but the subject of this negotiation is, in fact, the framework is Z-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that whatever press publication there has been, written by whomever, published wherever, which deals with these matters is for that reason where the witness could not add anything to that admissible evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No necessary, Your Honour, of course. But I would also refer to the witness testimony of Ambassador Galbraith on that portion as well, when he also said about the -- how Milan Martic was refusing the Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider whether or not to admit this in evidence. Mr. Registrar, the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D717, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D717 keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dangerfield, more than once in the course of your evidence, you emphasised that at the time of these events you were only 25, and that you experienced and viewed certain things differently from the way you do today. In that context, I would like to refer you to your own article, paragraph 3 on page 2, where you refer to the peace negotiations in Geneva, and you say: [In English] "My personal feelings were that I would actually like to be in war." Then you said: "I had missed out on the Gulf War; and if you do nothing else in the armed forces, it is undoubtedly the pinnacle of your career." [Interpretation] How are we to understand that you were actually wishing for a war and the breakdown of peace negotiations, in view of the duties you were performing for the forces of the United Nations which, by their nature, are peace forces?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why I joined the army. I didn't join the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Further on, in paragraph 4, you said: "I sat listening to the BBC World service news bulletin [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "... watching the BBC World news programme on Sky television, almost hoping that the talk would fail and break up. That way, I would almost certainly get the war that I hoped for." [Interpretation} Would you give us the same explanation for this statement?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would give the same explanation and I wouldn't change my mind today. After 16 years in the army, I left and I still didn't experience war. It is a regret that I never experienced it. I spent 16 years training, to do what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when the bombing of Knin began, so that was the war that you were wishing for and hoping for, then it must have been fun to you. At least on page 3, in the penultimate paragraph, you said: "It was, however, amusing eating my breakfast with helmet and a flak jacket on. Can we ascribe this statement to your youth, or was it really amusing to have a helmet and a flak jacket on during breakfast, during bombing?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the word "fun" would be wrong. I thought it was fantastic, and I thought it was quite an odd experience eating my breakfast wearing a helmet and flak jacket. I suppose the amusing part was when the initial bombardment came, I ran for the bunker clad only in a towel. That is the amusing bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, then, Mr. Dangerfield, you have raised this story yourself, this story with the towel, that is mentioned throughout different articles. But the fact is you had a jacket on. In fact, you had a jacket and your shoes that were carrying and that you had taken off before taking a shower, right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll get the order right. I got up, I had a shower, I was getting dry in my bedroom when the bombardment started. To save my dignity, I put a towel round myself, and I grabbed my helmet and my flak jacket and my webbing and my rifle and my pistol and my boots and my uniform, and I ran for the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. This topic is not so important as to waste precious court time on it. Let us move to another subject, which is important, and that's Grubori village. Mr. Dangerfield, page 6, paragraph 3 of your article from 1995, you say that: "In the morning on Saturday, 26 August, Andy ..." -- that was your driver. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You went to the Serb village Grubori in Plavno valley to the north-east of Knin. My first question about this would be: Why did you go to Grubori village, you and Andy, your driver?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fairly certain that we weren't the first members of the UN forces to go there, but I think there were either rumours or someone knew of it, and, therefore, I went up there for independent verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Grubori because it was your only decision or you received an order from your superior officers?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that you were accompanying Mr. Richard Bremford, who was working for UN Television. Was anyone else, apart from you, your driver Andy, and Mr. Richard Bremford, among the persons who arrived at the Grubori on the morning of the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm fairly certain I had a Canadian with me. It would almost certainly have been Phil Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] "As we draw into the village, you could smell the rancid fumes of houses that had been burned not 12 hours earlier. We were greeted by the most distressing site that I have ever witnessed. All women crying and wailing accompanied by three old men." [Interpretation] Do you recall how many they were, those elderly women you saw at Grubori?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] "We knew at once that something was dreadfully wrong. We discovered that night before the Croats had come, they had burned the village and slaughtered the men and livestock." [Interpretation] How did you discover that, that Croats had been in the village the night before?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Richard Bremford spoke fluent Serbo-Croat and Russian, I believe, and he had spoken to the villagers and that was the answer that he had got.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Had you received a report or did you observe personally how many men had been killed?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two men had been killed, and I describe that in the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, you say that when you entered a house, a woman showed you her husband lying face down on the floor in a pool of blood and that you saw two 7.62-millimetre casings. Then you go on to say: "The corpse was still fresh," and I will quote you: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "... seeped slowly across the floor." [Interpretation] Is this a good description of what you have seen, Mr. Dangerfield?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, in the course of your training, were given any lectures on the basic of forensics and crime investigation?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say towards the end of this paragraph, the man lying on the floor, [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... had had his throat slit." [Interpretation] How did you infer that the wound you describe occurred as a result of slitting the throat, not something else?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man was on the floor, there was a huge line across his throat, the flesh was parted, there was blood coming out of it, and that was a natural assumption for me to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you ever in your military service - and that includes later events; I mean later than 1995 - have occasion to see a wound caused by a bullet when it grazes the skin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We are given fairly regular medical training within the British Army, particularly prior to deploying on operations. We're shown all sorts of various different potential injuries, and we're all taught how to deal with them. Some of our young soldiers go on to do some fairly specialist training to deal with all sorts of different injuries that not everyone is capable of - not necessarily capable of - but particularly wants to do. So the standard of training has improved over the years and is very high; so, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you observed this scene, were you aware that you were actually on a scene that needs to be investigated by the police and their forensic teams?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, and that's where I refer to the improvements in our standard of train. The experiences learned by the British Army in Northern Ireland have been transferred over to the training that we have for all other theatres of operations; and. Therefore, in this day and age, yes, with the experience I have now, I most certainly would not have gone in there. I would have sealed the scene off for specialists to come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who else entered the room where this man was lying on the floor?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Richard Bremford with the television cameras was first in there; but I don't know who had been in before us in the morning, the day before, or, indeed, who went in there after us. I cannot account for those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Fair enough. [Interpretation] I apologise if my question was not understood; that means I did not put it very well. My question was and in fact, it should have been: At the moment, how many people were in the room where the corpse was lying on the floor?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the dead man. I think there was the two women. They were there for certain. I think standing at the doorway was the camera team, so I don't believe they were actually in the room at the time. And I would have been there with my driver, at the doorway possibly. And there would have been the other people who had met us as we arrived Grubori. But I'm fairly certain this Court would have seen the UN TV footage of the scene anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would have been approximately an hour but I cannot be certain. I didn't spend all that there, that was for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where you went after Grubori?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you inform anyone, any of your superiors or civilian authorities in Knin, about this?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I hadn't been asked to go there by any of my superiors in Knin, and I had discovered this place myself, I would have almost certainly informed them. But I had no liaison with the authorities in Knin. That was not for me; that was for the Canadian headquarters to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, before we continue with the aftermath of the visit, I would like it ask a few clarify questions. Mr. Dangerfield, you went to Grubori because there were rumours or you said there was something was happening there. How much time did it take to you get there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, sir, I can't remember whether it took an hour or two hours. I just don't know which route I took there, and I can't actually remember where it is in relation to Knin on a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say anything between one and two hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the road I went along and the tracks because, obviously, a good road could be very quick, a very poor track can take some time. I just simply can't give you an accurate answer on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my next question is: Did you learn from the people, Mr. Bremford was able to speak with, about when this had happened, this killing of the man that was found in his bedroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think we established that happened on the evening of the night before when we went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you described the corpse. May I take it that approximately what time did you leave; do you remember. You said in the morning, but it can be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I think we got there at 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning, something like that; and we would have been there an hour, so leaving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were looking at a corpse which as you describe was still fresh; but from what you tell me now, it must have -- the person must have been killed at least four to five hours, if not more before that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you're describing that the blood seeped slowly across the floor. Is that what you actually saw, that the blood was still -- I'm not a native speaking, but "seeping" means going taking a very slow course. After five six hours of a person had died, you saw the blood still slowly moving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, there was very thick pool of blood, and I'm fairly certain that it was moving slowly across the wooden floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We might have to verify that with data on coagulation of blood, which I just shared this with the parties. From what I learned about this in the past, in order to accept this, that would certainly need expert opinion. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way I'm looking at the clock. How long --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will be finished within five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes, that's accepted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, while you were on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, let me ask you, first of all, how long -- how much time did you spend in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In those two or three months, did you get to know some people that you had contact with, the locals as it were? I don't mean here members of the peacekeeping forces or some other agency which was not local on the territory of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether it was Croatia or Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Both. Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the British Army, we have always had a policy of getting to know the people whose country you're in, so it was important for me to establish relations within the community with anyone really. So, in the cafes, I would go in and have some particularly strong coffee. Occasionally, I was offered some slivovitz, just one. So, yes, it was very good to meet people, and, actually, you get a much better understanding of the situation. And I was fairly unique because I had had the experience with the Bosnians, I had had the experience in the Serb Krajina, and I had the experience with the Croatians. So I got to met everyone, and I felt very privileged to have had that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will quote your words, Mr. Dangerfield. This is on page 7 of your article, Exhibit P699, second paragraph. You say the following: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "... have behaved like animals. I do not side with the Serbs. The people from the Balkans are all bad as each other. Everything is about revenge." [Interpretation] Mr. Dangerfield, you wrote this when you were 25 years old. Now, from this perspective, have you been able to put a distance between your words then, that the Croats behaved like animals and that everybody was as bad as each other in the Balkans, meaning the people there?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I wrote this, I didn't expect it to be picked over 13 years ago -- 13 years later, rather. Some of the language is, indeed, strong; but, as I said, I was 25 and impressionable. So 13 years on, would I change what I had written, do I have a softer view?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] okay. [Interpretation] All right. Now -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was waiting for an answer to the question whether the witness had a softer view. He started thinking about it, and I think he wanted to share with us the outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was impressed with the clock hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Could you tell us whether you developed a softer view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my personal opinion only: I think you meddle in other people's business at your own peril. I have an understanding as to why people do things, but it's not for me to get hooked up in those views in this forum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you are not answering the question. Mr. Mikulicic, you have one minute extra.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I only one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you also quote Lord Clarendon, and you say the following [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] " ... a half ago, Lord Clarendon wrote: 'We are willing to do anything for the maintenance of peace, except committing ourselves to a policy of action.'" [Interpretation] And this is where your quote ends; however, Lord Clarendon's quote continues, and it reads [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "... after the policy of action," the quotation goes like this: "... that we could not justify and which would not be sanctioned by public opinion at home." [Interpretation] Is there any particular reason, Mr. Dangerfield, that you omitted the last portion of this quotation in your article?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Russo, could you give us an impression of how many time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Probably not more than five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Other parties, no. That means we will have some time left. And since today is the last day before the recess and since there is still quite a lot of MFIs to be dealt with, we will see how much time remains. So if every could be as prepared as good as possible, because we have not by received the final list by Mr. Registrar, to se what we can do. If we can't do it, perhaps we do it after the recess. We have a break until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, are you ready to re-examination the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President. Thank you. Mr. Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit D89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it, Mr. Kehoe, I think you still owed me a page and line reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do. The page and line reference was, in fact, the -- well, first of all, with regard to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about C3, and then the protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I checked. The Witness 56, he did not talk about C3, but C2 and C4. And with regard to Colonel Leslie's, the reference point, it was started off from his statement where he laid that out as this air defence battery being 300 metres south-west of the UN compound which led to the designation. Your Honour, you're 100 percent correct that he says with regard to that, on page 2130, at line 8 to 10: "The only reason I ask for a little bit of more specificity is I can't recall if that's the exact location of C3, the rebel anti-aircraft facility, but, yes." That is the high ground, Judge, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking argument at this moment. It's just where I could find the first point of reference you gave and where I informed you about what I found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had difficulties in going through three days of transcript to find the other reference, but now it's there, or it is not there, but that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, we have now the document on the screen. Apologies, Mr. Dangerfield, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if we could take this to the fourth page of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, if you recall, you were shown this exhibit by Mr. Kehoe and specifically directed to the second paragraph there, where it indicates ARSK soldiers of unknown strength were seen occupying defensive positions in general, area of Strmica, with the grid reference. Tanks and mortgages were seen in the same positions. And then at 05, 1815, they fired 12 rounds of arty from Strmica towards Knin. Mr. Dangerfield, you were a regimental tank commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you had been to Strmica prior to Operation Storm. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Court whether or not a tank firing from Strmica could reach Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the direct fire roll, no; in the indirect fire roll, extremely unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you explain the distinction, please?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the direct fire role, that would have been the tank commander being able to visually see his target, so he has to have line of sight. And, certainly, from my experience, that maximum range is about two kilometres in the direct fire role. In the indirect fire role, you would elevate the gun to an angle of evaluation similar to how an artillery fire piece fires up in the air. This is a technique certainly in the British Army we don't practice anymore; but I know that if we were to fire out that range, the maximum range we could achieve is ten kilometres, and I believe the distance from Strmica to Knin is considerably more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Court whether mortars could reach from Strmica to Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know an 80-millimetre mortar probably has a range of about 5.650 metres; 120-millimetre mortar might go out to about ten or 12 kilometres. But, again, a mortar, I don't believe, could reach Knin from Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to speak with any of the Kenyan Battalion officers who had manned the Strmica point any time after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dangerfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further yeses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need for further questions. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just briefly. Further cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, you don't even know what weapons systems when it comes to mortars they were using because this report doesn't have it, does it?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That report that I have just seen says "mortars."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You don't know what type of mortar -- what -- what level of mortar they had, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maximum size mortar they could have had was 120-millimetre, and that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, excuse me. The question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could you please allow the witness to finish his answer. You said the maximum size of mortar they could have had was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was 120-millimetre, sir, so that couldn't have reached Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The maximum mortar size was 120, and who had 120? Is it your testimony that the ARSK had a 120 -- the maximum range of an ARSK mortar was with 120-millimetre. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you say that, again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You said to us, in direct examination, that the maximum range on a mortar was ten to 12 kilometres, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do you know -- do you know, as you sit here, if those mortars were being fired into Knin from a range of ten to 12 kilometres? As you sit here, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were. I was questioned on the report that you put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And based on the report, you have no idea what the ARSK was actually firing, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that at the range, they couldn't have reached Knin. I'm not saying I knew what they were firing; I'm just saying the range was too great for them to reach Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is: Based on the report, you have no idea what of ARSK was actually firing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe, that's what the witness said several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the apparent issue was whether the projectiles that were fired at that moment could have possibly reached Knin. Now we have two categories. One was dealt with, that's the tank direct fire, indirect fire; then we have mortars. Now, the witness, for one reason or another, tells us that the maximum range for a mortar - that means whatever mortar you fire, it could never reach any further - would be ten to 12 kilometres, and he referred to 120-millimetre mortars. Mr. Dangerfield, are you aware of any higher calibre mortars than 120-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that on which you base your answer that with the heaviest charge of 120-millimetre, that the range would be at a maximum ten to 12 kilometres, and that, therefore, considering tanks and/or mortars, that neither of them could have fired and have reached Knin from the position where they were observed to have been seen firing? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now we have a clear answer. Mr. Kehoe, any further questions about this matter to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just one last question: Mr. Dangerfield, you do not know what the ARSK was actually firing at, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND CHARLES DAVID DANGERFIELD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, apart from the report that says towards Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench has no further questions to you, Mr. Dangerfield. You may have noticed that they came already in between. Since the party have no questions either, this conclude your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for answering the questions put to you by the parties and the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Dangerfield out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said, before the break, that I would like to try and deal with some MFIs. Having reviewed this during the break, the lists that were provided to the parties were provided to them only very recently. I did not find time to go through the lists and having all the details ready to further discuss them with you. Therefore, I think, as a matter of fact, that if we would deal with the MFI at this moment, that we would waste more time in being confused than that we would get quickly to a result. If the parties consider that there's any specific document that we should deal with before the recess, then I'd like to hear. Otherwise, I'd like to invite the parties to well prepare for any moment shortly after the recess to deal with that and get the list again as short as the list once was. Is there any other procedural matter which needs attention at this moment, and I remind you of the fact that we'll not see each other for four weeks. Nothing. Mr. Russo, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Tieger is not there to spoil the quiet atmosphere. This means that we will take an early break. We then will adjourn and we'll resume in four weeks from now. That will be, if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Registrar, the 25th of August. Yes, it is Monday, the 25th of August and we'll be in at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in Courtroom II. I wish you at least some relaxation during the recess. Of course, I'm aware that, for the accused, that that is not the situation which you wish to be in during the summer holidays. The Chamber is fully aware of that. I hope to see you all back in good health on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th of August, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
